competitors.name: Planbook.com (+ Planbook Mobile)
competitors.model: Paid subscription — $20/1yr, $36/2yr, $48/3yr (in-app purchase tiers listed on the iOS App Store); ~$18/license for bulk school orders
competitors.note: The category incumbent — markets itself as 1M+ teachers and 1B+ lessons. Rated 4.8 from 7.3K iOS ratings. Its headline feature is exactly our pain point: it auto-bumps plans forward on a snow day. Requires an account (SSO/biometric login), is cloud-hosted, and its store listing says nothing about offline use. Weakness: the mobile app is buggy around the bulk operations specials teachers live on.

competitors.name: PlanbookEdu
competitors.model: $25/yr per Capterra reviewers; also listed at $20/teacher/yr and $30/yr Premium. Free tier exists but is limited
competitors.note: Web-only, explicitly requires 'a web browser, a Mac or PC, and an internet connection.' Supports A/B rotations. Reviewers consistently call the UI 'old-school' and 'clunky,' and printing is a repeated failure. This is the most directly beatable competitor.

competitors.name: Planboard (by Chalk, now owned by PowerSchool)
competitors.note: The one tool teachers specifically recommend to specials teachers because it accommodates rotation schedules and non-standard specialist timetables, plus device sync. Claims 250K+ teachers. Risk to them (opportunity for us): Chalk was absorbed into PowerSchool's enterprise curriculum products, which historically means drift toward district sales and away from the free individual teacher.

competitors.name: iDoceo
competitors.model: $19.99 one-time purchase, no subscription, no IAP
competitors.note: Genuinely good rotating-cycle support — has a documented 'configure a rotating day cycle in your calendar' workflow and lets you bump lessons. Fatal gap: Apple-only (iPad/iPhone/Mac). Developer has stated on their own forum there are no plans for Android or PC 'in the near future.' Every Chromebook and Android teacher — i.e. most of US K-12 — is locked out.

competitors.name: Common Planner (formerly Common Curriculum)
competitors.model: Freemium — 'free forever' individual tier; Pro for Teachers $5.59/mo billed annually
competitors.note: Rebranded and repositioned around AI lesson generation. Clean, modern, collaboration-friendly. Account required and it is now an AI-forward product, which means district data-vetting friction for many teachers.

competitors.name: Planbook Plus
competitors.note: Cheaper minor player; supports sharing planbooks between teachers. Low mindshare.

competitors.name: TPT / blog printables (e.g. Mrs. J in the Library 'Simple Lesson Planner & Calendar for Fixed or Flexible Library Schedules')
competitors.model: Paid one-off, typically $3-8, or free with email signup
competitors.note: THE real competitor for this exact niche. An editable Word .doc on legal-size paper with a line per week or 'cycle,' sold specifically because 'a rotating 6-day cycle is hard to track digitally.' It wins on being undated and shift-proof; it loses because it is paper, unsearchable, and dies if you lose it.

competitors.name: Google Sheets / Excel (self-rolled)
competitors.note: The true default. Music and PE teachers build one sheet with a tab per grade covering the whole year, reused across years. Wins: infinitely flexible, free, no vetting, offline-ish. Loses: nobody builds the cycle-day math, so every snow day means manually re-dragging rows, and it is unusable on a phone in a hallway.

complaints.complaint: 'Scheduling on a rotating teaching schedule such as a 6-day cycle is hard to track digitally, and every time there's a snow day or school cancellation, the dates for your next lessons change, which can disrupt your lesson or unit flow because where the weekend or school breaks happen also changes.'
complaints.source: Mrs. J in the Library, sales copy for her printable specials/library lesson planner — she is literally selling paper because software fails at this
complaints.weWinIf: We store lessons against CYCLE POSITION, not calendar dates. Dates are a rendered view. A one-tap 'no school today' pushes the entire cycle forward and every class's next lesson follows automatically, with an undo. This is the single most important feature in the app and should be on the home screen, not buried in settings.

complaints.complaint: 'It is disappointing that problems with the copy/paste a lesson feature wasn't able to be resolved... The time of each class the lesson is pasted to will change, then you have to go in and reset the time of the class.'
complaints.source: Planbook Mobile, iOS App Store review dated 3/4/2024
complaints.weWinIf: Copying one lesson to many sections is our core verb, not an edge case. Pasting must carry the lesson content and inherit the destination section's own time slot — never overwrite it. Ship a 'apply to all sections of this grade' action that touches 6 classes in one tap.

complaints.complaint: 'The app is a little more touchy... I've been unable to create events on the app... I get an error telling me to pick a valid start time, but nothing is wrong with the time I pick.'
complaints.source: Planbook Mobile, iOS App Store review dated 2/24/2025
complaints.weWinIf: No validation error may ever be un-actionable. Prefer inputs that cannot produce an invalid state (pickers over free text), and if we must reject input, say exactly which field and why, inline. Better: autosave partial state so nothing is ever lost to a validation wall.

complaints.complaint: 'Plans did not print well' and became 'difficult to read' when substantial content was included, requiring multiple pages for a single day.
complaints.weWinIf: Print is a first-class output, not an afterthought. Ship a real @media print stylesheet with a one-week-per-page layout, tested and toggleable between 'compact grid' and 'full detail.' Offer letter and legal. Admins still ask specials teachers for printed plans — this is a weekly ritual we can own outright.

complaints.complaint: A teacher wished for 'more different colors' to designate classes, as existing options 'look too similar.'
complaints.weWinIf: A specials teacher has 25-30 sections, not 5. We need a palette engineered for many simultaneous, mutually distinguishable, colorblind-safe classes — and we should color by GRADE LEVEL by default (6 hues, high separation) with section distinguished by label/shade, which is how their brain actually groups it.

complaints.complaint: 'Some of the features can be a little clunky or old-school to relocate/duplicate/fill/edit' and 'deleting a series of days in a row is cumbersome.'
complaints.weWinIf: Bulk operations by default: multi-select days/sections, drag a lesson across the grid, and range-delete. Every destructive bulk action gets one undo toast rather than a confirm dialog.

complaints.complaint: Extending plans could delete previous content if the academic year was already full — i.e. silent data loss.
complaints.weWinIf: Never destroy on overflow. Local-first storage with an explicit versioned autosave, a visible 'last saved' indicator, and a one-file JSON export so a teacher's entire year can be backed up and restored by hand. Data loss in a planner is unforgivable and is our best trust wedge.

complaints.complaint: The platform 'can be slow at times, especially when paging through multiple weeks.'
complaints.weWinIf: Static PWA with everything in IndexedDB means week-paging is instant and works with the wifi off. Make speed visible: no spinners anywhere in normal navigation.

complaints.complaint: 'Planbook does not offer as many customization options for the planbook as some users would like, and editing the planbook after it is created is not possible.'
complaints.weWinIf: Schedule structure must be editable forever. Specials schedules get rebuilt mid-year constantly (new section added, rotation changed after winter break). Changing the cycle length or a section's slot must never require starting a new planbook.

complaints.complaint: iDoceo 'is not a web app and won't run on Windows or Android devices,' and the developer confirmed on their own forum they have 'no plans to develop iDoceo for PC or Android in the near future,' despite repeated teacher requests.
complaints.source: iDoceo official forum thread 'Android or PC' and iDoceo site
complaints.weWinIf: We are a browser PWA. Chromebook, Android, iPad, Windows desktop, all identical, installable to home screen. For US K-12 — a Chromebook monoculture — this alone beats the best rotating-cycle tool on the market.

complaints.complaint: PlanbookEdu requires 'a web browser, a Mac or PC, and an internet connection'; Planbook's store listing makes no offline claim. School wifi in a gym, an art room, or a library annex is notoriously bad.
complaints.source: PlanbookEdu marketing copy; Planbook Mobile App Store listing
complaints.weWinIf: Full offline via service worker, stated plainly on the landing page: 'Works with the wifi off.' A PE teacher outside on a field with no signal is a real, common, weekly scenario for this exact user.

complaints.complaint: Teachers are warned that signing students up for an app 'might actually be violating FERPA,' that un-vetted tools get blocked from district devices, and that vetting can be lengthy enough that you should 'redesign your lesson or project plan' around the delay.
complaints.source: Future of Privacy Forum 'Educator's Guide to Student Privacy'; ConnectSafely educator privacy guide; US DoE Student Privacy office guidance
complaints.weWinIf: Our stance becomes the marketing. No account, no upload, nothing leaves the device, and — critically — the app never asks for a student name at all. It tracks SECTIONS ('3rd - Ms. Alvarez'), not rosters. That means there is no student data, so there is nothing to vet. Say this in one sentence at the top of the page.

tableStakes: Rotating cycle support as a first-class concept — Day 1-6, A/B, or 4-week rotations — not a Monday-through-Friday grid with a workaround. This is the entry ticket; without it we are not in the category.
One-tap 'bump' / shift-everything-forward when school is cancelled, with undo. Planbook advertises this by name; its absence is instantly disqualifying.
Copy or duplicate one lesson across many sections at once, and across weeks. The defining action of the job.
Clean print / PDF export of a week's plans that fits on one page and stays legible — admins still ask for printed plans.
Per-class color coding with enough genuinely distinguishable colors for 25+ sections.
Attach links and material notes to a lesson (URL, file name, 'get the djembes from the closet').
A standards field — even a free-text or paste-in one. Every credible planner has it and admins ask for it.
Autosave that survives reload and browser close, with a visible saved state.
Data export/backup and re-import — the only honest substitute for cloud sync when there are no accounts.
Per-section pacing memory: 'where did I leave off with THIS class,' since sections of the same grade drift apart within a week.
differentiators: Cycle-first data model. Lessons are pinned to cycle position (Day 3, Period 2), and the calendar is a rendered projection. Nobody in the paid tier does this properly — it is why teachers still buy a Word doc from a blog. This makes the snow-day bump nearly free to implement and makes the whole app correct-by-construction.

A 'What did each class get?' matrix: sections down, lessons across. This is the spreadsheet teachers hand-build and no app ships. One screen answers the actual daily question. Cheap to build, immediately recognizable, screenshot-able for word of mouth.

Hallway Mode / Now-Next: the app opens to an enormous, high-contrast card showing the class walking in right now, the lesson, the materials line, and where that specific section left off. One thumb, five seconds, standing next to a cart. Everything else is one tap away.

Teach-once, vary-per-section: author a lesson once for '3rd grade,' auto-assign to all six 3rd-grade sections, then log a per-section deviation ('3B didn't finish printmaking — start there next time') without forking the lesson. Directly serves the drift problem.

No student names, ever — by design, not omission. Sections only. Put it in the copy: 'There is no student data in this app, so there is nothing for your district to vet.' Turns our constraint into the single strongest trust claim in a FERPA-nervous category.
Full offline, installable, works on a Chromebook. Beats iDoceo (Apple-only) and PlanbookEdu (internet required) simultaneously, at zero marginal cost to us.

One-file year backup: export the whole year as a single JSON (and a human-readable printout), import on any device. Honest 'sync' without accounts, and doubles as the year-over-year reuse feature — specials teachers explicitly reuse last year's sheet.

Hand-off export straight into our existing Sub Plans app. A specials sub plan is uniquely painful (six different grades in one day) and we already own the other half. Cross-links two portfolio apps for free.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The paid incumbents (Planbook, PlanbookEdu) look like web-1.5 spreadsheets: dense grids, small type, thin borders, muted institutional blue/gray chrome, desktop-first tables that collapse badly on a phone. Reviewers call this 'clunky' and 'old-school' unprompted. The newer wave (Common Planner) has gone clean-minimal and AI-forward — generous whitespace, rounded cards, big primary CTAs, mobile-first — which is the current direction of edtech UI generally (minimalism, large tap targets, consistent nav, role-based dashboards rather than one generic user view). The other pole is the TPT/teacher-blog aesthetic: script fonts, rainbow chevrons, apple and pencil clipart, faux-paper and washi-tape textures, pastel everything. DATED: skeuomorphic leather/paper planner textures, that TPT rainbow-cutesy look, tiny 12px grid cells, hover-dependent controls, and modal-heavy editing. CURRENT AND RIGHT FOR US: calm minimal, generous type scale, real cards, obvious tap targets, color used as information (which grade) rather than decoration. Important nuance from the research: many teachers come from traditional settings and respond to layouts that echo their familiar charts and planbooks — so we want the SHAPE of a planbook grid with modern type, spacing, and contrast, not a wholesale abstract redesign.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: There are two completely distinct modes and the app must serve both. MODE 1 — the hallway, which is 90% of sessions. A specials teacher runs about six 50-minute classes a day, sees 500-750 students, and has roughly five minutes between classes; a large share of them teach from a rolling cart with no room of their own and are physically pushing it down a corridor. They are standing, moving, holding a phone or tablet in one hand, surrounded by noise, often with a line of second-graders already forming. They open the app to answer exactly one question: 'who is walking in, what am I doing with them, and where did we leave off?' That demands: a single enormous glanceable card, minimum 18-20px body and much larger for the class name, very high contrast (art rooms and gyms have terrible glare and inconsistent light), tap targets at 48px+, zero hover dependence, no precision drag required, and no state that can be lost by the screen locking mid-task. MODE 2 — Sunday evening at the kitchen table, laptop, coffee, a low-grade dread about the week. Calmer, willing to type, wants the grid, wants bulk copy, wants to print. This mode tolerates density; the hallway mode absolutely does not. Underneath both: this is a chronically undervalued role ('specials' teachers are often treated as the prep-coverage machine) with an absurd student-count-to-planning-time ratio. The app should feel like it respects the craft and reduces load — never chirpy, never gamified, never adding a task.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: calm, sturdy, warm, generous, uncluttered, quietly creative

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Warm terracotta / clay — a muted earthenware orange-red (roughly hue 12-20°, moderate chroma), paired with a deep warm charcoal-brown ground and a soft bone/paper off-white surface. Grade levels then get a 6-hue categorical ramp derived around it (clay, marigold, sage, slate-teal, plum, deep ochre) chosen for colorblind separation, since 25+ sections is the real constraint.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Terracotta is the material of the specials wing — kiln clay, craft paper, gym floor lacquer, the warm wood of an Orff xylophone. It reads 'arts and making' to this exact user without a single piece of clipart, and it carries warmth and steadiness rather than urgency. Emotionally it is the right temperature for someone who is overloaded: warm hues feel supportive and human where blue-gray institutional chrome feels like more administrative burden piled on. It is also strongly differentiated inside a 23-app portfolio — earthy warm reds are an unusual pick and will be instantly recognizable on a home screen next to the more common blues, greens, and grays. Practically, a muted clay works well as a large-surface color at low chroma (headers, the now-next card) and darkens cleanly to a text-safe shade. NOTE: bring the base clay down to roughly the 40-45% lightness range before using it for text or thin icons on the bone background — at its natural saturation it will fail 4.5:1, so define a separate darker 'clay-ink' token for text and keep the bright clay for fills and 3px+ marks. In dark mode invert to a warm near-black ground with a lightened clay accent rather than desaturating to gray, or the whole personality drains out.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Avoid edtech blue at all costs — Planbook, Google Classroom, Seesaw, ClassDojo, and half the district portal software are all blue, and it is the single most invisible choice here. Avoid schoolhouse red plus apple plus chalkboard-green, the clip-art cliché that instantly reads amateur. Avoid the TPT pastel rainbow / script-font aesthetic; it is beloved by a slice of the audience but it caps the app's perceived seriousness and looks dated fast. Avoid green as the primary identity — in a teacher tool green and red are semantically loaded as pass/fail and grading, and we are not a gradebook. Avoid pure gray-neutral minimalism, which will read as 'another district compliance tool.' Accessibility watch-outs: do not distinguish grade levels by hue alone (add a persistent grade label or shape), and do not put mid-value clay text on the bone surface without darkening it first.

confidence: Medium-high overall, with specific gaps worth naming. HIGH CONFIDENCE: competitor pricing (Planbook's $20/$36/$48 tiers read directly off the iOS App Store IAP list; iDoceo's $19.99 one-time and its no-Android stance confirmed on iDoceo's own site and forum; PlanbookEdu ~$20-25/yr and Common Planner's $5.59/mo-annual free-plus-Pro structure). HIGH CONFIDENCE on the complaint texture from Capterra (PlanbookEdu printing, clunky bulk edit, too-few colors, slow paging, overflow data loss) and from two dated iOS reviews of Planbook Mobile (copy/paste time bug, phantom start-time validation error) — these are verbatim. HIGH CONFIDENCE on the rotating-cycle/snow-day-drift pain, which is stated plainly in the sales copy of a printable planner sold specifically to library/specials teachers, and corroborated by the fact that Planbook advertises auto-bump as a headline feature. HIGH CONFIDENCE on the physical context: six 50-minute classes a day, ~750 students, five minutes between classes comes from a first-person specials-rotation librarian account, and cart-teaching logistics are well documented across music-ed sources. NOT VERIFIED — call these out: (1) I could NOT get Reddit. Both reddit.com and old.reddit.com are blocked from this tool, and the search engine returned nothing usable for site-restricted Reddit queries, so there is no r/Teachers or r/MusicEd primary-source sentiment in here. The complaint set is Capterra + App Store + teacher blogs + vendor copy instead. If you want Reddit texture, that is a manual pass someone should do. (2) ProTeacher's Planbook.com thread returned 403, so I have the thread's existence but not its contents. (3) Google Play's Planboard listing truncated before reviews/installs, so Planboard's current rating, review sentiment, and whether it still handles rotations well post-PowerSchool are unverified — the 'accommodates rotation schedules' claim comes from a roundup, not from testing. Planboard is the competitor most worth someone actually signing up for and poking at, since it is free and aimed at the same rotation problem. (4) Common Planner's exact free-tier feature limits are unverified; the pricing page truncated on fetch. (5) I found no direct evidence of teachers complaining that Planbook lacks offline access — I inferred the weakness from PlanbookEdu's own 'requires an internet connection' copy and the absence of any offline claim in Planbook's store listing. Treat 'offline is a competitive gap' as strongly implied, not user-attested. (6) The color recommendation assumes terracotta is unclaimed in the existing 23-app portfolio; I did not inspect the other apps' palettes, so check for collision before committing.
